L-R: Bruce Barth, David Ambrosio and Donny McCaslin Camara, Sidiki: Ankaben They say : Malian-born, Oslo-based percussionist and cultural ambassador Sidiki Camara is set to release Ankaben, his most ambitious project to date, bringing together an extraordinary ensemble of Norwegian jazz, folk and contemporary musicians. (Oslo Session Recordings (OSR) and the number of the album is OSR010. The irc code for the single Ankaben is: NOTJK2609001) Cappel, Tristan: Constellations They say : North Star, the sophomore album from Los Angeles-based composer and multi-instrumentalist Tristan Cappel, arrives June 18 as eight original compositions exploring grief, self-actualization, and the act of following one’s inner guiding light. The core ensemble — Adam Hersh (piano, Rhodes, synths), Max Gerl (bass), Alex Sill (guitar), and Myles Martin (drums) — is joined on select tracks by notable Los Angeles figures Miguel Atwood-Ferguson, Telemakus, and Andrew Renfroe. (Independent) Hear Tristan Cappel . Carter, Ron & Silberstein, Yotam: Duets They say : Bassist Ron Carter, approaching his 89th birthday, and Israeli-born New York guitarist Yotam Silberstein pay tribute to Carter’s celebrated duo recordings with the late Jim Hall on Duets, released on JOJO Records. Recorded at Rudy Van Gelder’s Englewood Cliffs studio, coincidentally on Hall’s birthday, the eight-track set mixes standards, including Brazilian and jazz songbook material, with two Silberstein originals, Blues for Brother Malone and the waltz Rain Again. (Jojo Records) Hear Ron Carter & Yotam Silberstein Cartwright, Deirdre: Organik They say : Deirdre Cartwright returns with Organik, her first album in 15 years, reflecting her influences while introducing new work. Joined by Pete Whittaker (Hammond organ) and Gary Hammond (percussion), she strips back her sound, playing without effects for a warm, resonant tone. The album combines fine reinterpretations, including ‘Eleanor Rigby’, with original compositions and tributes to Emily Remler and others, moving between swing, Latin and blues-infused grooves with imagination and a strong sense of trio interplay. (Blow The Fuse Records – BTF2616CD) Cederbaum, Fella: Aliens Are Watching They say : Aliens Are Watching, Fella Cederbaum third poetry album with original music is an invitation to step outside ourselves and observe humanity through the eyes of an outside observer. Through a collection of thought-provoking spoken-word pieces, Fella Cederbaum holds up a mirror to all of us. Rather than offering answers, she invites listeners to an immersive journey of unflinching self-discovery. Her poems are reflections in the form of rigorous, provocative, at times humorous, even sarcastic socio-spiritual commentary, devoid of opinion and personal preference. (MahniVerse Productions digital only) Chadwick, James: Walrws They say : The band play a range of classic pop tunes from the 60s with a Jazz Twist and in the realms of contemporary Jazz, and while essence of the original has stayed the same the quartet have given the tunes an added spontaneity and care free outlook through re harmonisations. Liz Exell – Drums, Mark Sambell – Piano, Aidan Thorne Double Bass, Josh Heaton – Saxophone, James Chadwick Guitar/ arranger. (33 records 321) Hear James Chadwick . Cherry, Don + Brand, Dollar + Ward, Carlos: The Third World-Underground They say : First-ever international release of the legendary collaboration between Abdullah Ibrahim (Dollar Brand) and Don Cherry, featuring Carlos Ward. Recorded live in 1972 at Jazzhus Montmartre in Copenhagen, this highly sought-after album was originally released exclusively in Japan in 1974 on the cult jazz label Trio Records via its revered Nadja imprint. (Wewantsounds WWSCD125) Chevillon, Bruno: Etats De Lieux They say : A solo encounter between a double bass, a Paris church, and twelve luminous states of being. Invited in September 2011 by sound engineer Philippe Teissier du Cros, double bassist Bruno Chevillon spent two days improvising alone in the Lutheran Protestant Church of Bon Secours in Paris. The building is as much a protagonist as the player — its acoustics shaping every bow stroke, every silence. Twelve tracks traverse extremes: commanding attacks that send sonorities boomeranging through the nave. (Blaser Music SONGS005CD CD) Civil Disobedience (David Ambrosio, Donny McCaslin, Ingrid Jensen, Bruce Barth & Victor Lewis) – Civil Disobedience: Blue Note in the Progressive ’60s They say : Bassist David Ambrosio leads a quintet with saxophonist Donny McCaslin, trumpeter Ingrid Jensen, pianist Bruce Barth and drummer Victor Lewis on Civil Disobedience: Blue Note in the progressive 60s, released on Blue Frog Records. The album revives shelved late-1960s Blue Note repertoire by Bobby Hutcherson, James Spaulding, Joe Chambers and Harold Land tied to the civil rights era, including Spaulding’s A Time to Go, a tribute to Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. (Blue Frog Records) Hear Civil Disobedience . Cohen Almonte Duo: Timelines They say : Two-guitar debut from Tomer Cohen and Rodrigo Almonte. Timelines blends contemporary jazz improvisation with Andean, Brazilian, Mediterranean and Middle Eastern inflexions. The music centres on lyrical melodies, rhythmic interplay and chamber-like textures, moving from delicate ballads to energetic exchanges. For people interested in modern guitar duos, cross-cultural jazz, folk-rooted harmony and improvisation shaped by touch, rhythm and dialogue. (Adhyâropa Records ÂR00150 / ÂREU0012) Hear Cohen Almonte Duo . Cohen, Josh: We Are Home They say : After years of redefining what a solo electric bass can do, Josh Cohen opens his musical world to collaboration on We Are Home. His first ensemble album as a bandleader blends contemporary jazz, fusion, progressive writing, deep grooves, and lyrical melody. Featuring Jeremy Ledbetter, Lucian Gray, Rob Christian, and Mateo Mancuso, the recording explores family, transition, belonging, and the creative relationships that transform a place into home in Cohen’s evolving artistic journey and life. (T.Sound (TSND-004)) Córas Trio: Birth Is Upon Me, Death Is Upon Me They say : Córas Trio return with the follow-up to their critically acclaimed debut, continuing their distinctive blend of improvised avant folk, electronic experimentation and Irish traditional music. Belfast-based musicians Kevin McCullagh (fiddle, electronics), Paddy McKeown (guitar, electronics) and Conor McAuley (drums) deepen the trio’s fusion of tradition, improvisation and electronics, using the studio to shape spontaneous performances. Fiddle, guitar, percussion and musique concrète textures explore impermanence, transformation and renewal. (Coracle CR003) Curtis, Caleb Wheeler and Jason Moran: Incantation They say : The deeply attuned duo of multi-instrumentalist Caleb Wheeler Curtis and pianist Jason Moran delve into the tradition of great jazz duos while pressing ever forward, embracing the music’s spirit of creativity and invention. Through original compositions, free improvisation, and favorite tunes, the duo invokes and honors great jazz artists of the past while planting themselves firmly in the present, offering scintillating proof that jazz is alive and thriving. (Imani Records) D’Angelo, Andrew: BCDeluxe They say : Alto saxophonist and bass clarinetist Andrew D’Angelo presents BCDELUXE, a solo statement out September 18 on Jakob Bro’s Loveland Music, extending the label’s solo series that has featured Mark Turner, Thomas Morgan and Palle Mikkelborg. Produced by D’Angelo, Peter Karl and Bro, the album arrives as D’Angelo, who has written openly about living with a brain tumor, steps back from live performance. The LP is limited to 300 copies with artwork by Tal R. (Loveland Music) Hear Andrew D’Angelo . Dautch, Saul & Cowan, Bryan: Downward Current They say : NYC-based baritone saxophonists, Saul Dautch (Delray Beach, FL) and Bryan Cowan (Scranton, PA) began their association in 2023 upon both being named as one of “The Futures of the Baritone Saxophone” by the Low Blow Society of NYC (founded by Downbeat Award-winning baritone saxophonist Gary Smulyan). Collaboration came easy, as both Dautch and Cowan found that their improvisational and compositional styles had a nice contrast and synergy. Their debut recording, Downward Current represents their maiden voyage as a band leading duo. (NOOX [0120]) Dayyyani, Antonio: Organisme They say : Danish drummer and composer Antonio Dayyani returns with Organisme, the third album from his sextet and a portrait of a band shaped by collaboration, movement and constant evolution. Blending modern jazz with influences from americana, rock and open improvisation, the album captures a defining period in the ensemble’s development following a year of touring across Denmark and Europe. (April Records) Di, Ruta: Onwards & Upwards They say : Widely known for her virtuosity and dexterity on both guitar and vocals, Ruta Di pairs wonderfully tasteful solos with infectious hooks. Japanese jazz magazine The Walkers described her as “a hot topic for her exceptional guitar playing”,highlighting her distinctive presence as both an instrumentalist and bandleader. Ruta’s music has received support and recognition from platforms including BBC Radio, Jazz FM, D’Angelico Guitars and Women in Jazz. (Independent) Dickson, Jim: First Light They say : Debut solo piano album from San Diego pianist Jim Dickson. Eight original compositions spanning samba, fast Harlem stride, walking-bass blues, Latin jazz, contemplative ballad, and rhythm changes. Title track “First Light” inspired by Oscar Peterson’s “Hymn to Freedom.” “Chucho’s Tide” tips the hat to Chucho Valdés. Recorded on a Baldwin Model M baby grand with two pencil-condenser microphones. Mastered by Maria Triana. Solo piano throughout. ( youtube.com/@jimdicksonpiano ) Hear Jim Dickson . Dolphy, Eric: Out There They say : Eric Dolphy’s second LP as a leader, taped in 1960 the same year he recorded his debut LP, ‘Outward Bound’. Although these were his first recordings as a leader, Dolphy was already a veteran with considerable recording experience. He had formed part of drummer Roy Porter’s orchestra during 1948-1950, and in 1949 he made his first recording with Charles Mingus. Instrumentation on Out There is unusual, with Dolphy playing in a quartet that features Ron Carter on cello. (Pan Am Records 9152345 LP) Donaldson, John: We Were Together, I Forget The Rest They say : After a career spanning more than five decades, acclaimed British pianist and composer John Donaldson brings together a remarkable cast of collaborators and friends (including Norma Winstone, Rob Luft, and Jeff Ballard) for We Were Together, I Forget the Rest – a deeply personal new album written in memory of his late wife, Agatha Coffey. (Hexagonal Records) Duchess: A Marvelous Party They say : Duchess: Acclaimed vocalists Amy Cervini, Hilary Gardner, and Melissa Stylianou join forces and voices to become Duchess, a New York City-based vocal trio known for tight harmonies and big fun, carrying the tradition of the Boswell and Andrews Sisters into the 21st century. Duchess’s new album chooses joy without pretending the world is any less complicated or any less in turmoil. Across a program arranged by producer Oded Lev-Ari for swinging rhythm and horn sections. (A-Train / Anzic Records ANZ009602 CD) Dworak, Kuba: Roots They say : Polish double bassist Kuba Dworak announces the release of Roots, a deeply personal solo album that reaches across generations, drawing on the living memory of a family uprooted by war, economic hardship, and the cruel luck of history — and finding in music a way home. (Independent) Hear Kuba Dworak . The Republic of Ireland's Nations League game against Israel will go ahead tomorrow. At a rescheduled pre-match press conference in Hungary this afternoon, Manager Heimir Hallgrimsson confirmed one of the players has pulled out of the squad. It had been in doubt after this morning's press conference was postpone and a team meeting was called. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c574.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, A vandalised shopfront in Paris in the aftermath of protests By James Waterhouse ,Â Paris correspondent Â and Â Gabriela Pomeroy Published 18 minutes ago France awoke to scenes of widespread damage on Sunday after a day of riots and demonstrations, with shopfronts shattered, burnt out cars, charred bikes, and piles of glass and debris on the pavements of Paris. Police arrested about 1,800 people on Saturday as some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for protests that were largely peaceful. They were demonstrating against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools. Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings. Image source, Reuters Image caption, The destroyed interior of a restaurant in the capital on Sunday morning Widespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas. In Paris, protesters clashed with riot police, who turned tear gas and water cannon on the crowds. During the day, some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles. At least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups. Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons. Further south in Marseille, protesters broke into the city hall by using a metal fence as a battering ram. In Lille a McDonalds was set on fire, police said, and an Apple store in the city was broken into and looted. Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu said 150 police officers were injured in the unrest. On Sunday morning in Paris, residents surveyed the damage, which included the smashed glass frontages of designer stores including Ralph Lauren, Gucci and Versace. Shopkeepers were out early with brooms, picking up large shards of glass as they began the clean-up. Rubbish trucks worked their way down some of the larger streets to clear some of the debris. Many shops were daubed with graffiti, some reading "tax the rich" and "eat the rich." The BBC visited a clothes shop close to the Place de la RÃ©publique which had been ransacked, with piles of clothes and furniture scattered across the shop floor. The shop's distraught owner told the BBC he saw looters on the CCTV who were in the shop for just over an hour and a half, and that during that time he saw no police in the process. The owner - who asked not to be identified - told the BBC he did not believe any of those who robbed the shop were genuine protesters against school conditions or the cost of living. He said the looters were taking advantage of the demonstrations. CCTV footage shown on France's Channel 2 shows groups of teenagers, mostly wearing masks, in a shop selling mobile phones helping themselves to items from the shelves. Figure caption, Watch: How day of protests unfolded on Saturday as disorder broke out across France Student protests in France have seen hundreds of thousands take to the streets since they began late last month. Protesters have been demanding additional investment in their schools, criticising the lack of teachers and staff, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings. In the city of Lyon, Mayor GrÃ©gory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy", telling French outlet BFMTV that "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building". Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze. Fire crews also battled a fire at Limoges town hall, which caused part of the building to collapse. Local officials said the town hall was "largely lost." "A wild horde" had "deliberately" set fire to the 143-year-old building, said Maurice Barate, the prefect for the Haute-Vienne department. Elsewhere, a young man "had his hand blown off" by a small explosive in Saint-Ãtienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor RÃ©gis Juanico said on social media. "Such a tragedy should never have happened," he said. Image source, Reuters Image caption, A woman jogs past burnt out vehicles in Paris, near the Place de la RÃ©publique France's interior ministry said Saturday's protests involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in places, including parts of the capital and also in Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse, and the western city of Angers. Damage to buildings was reported across France, including in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence.
